4.2.4. Test-phase likeability ratings
A supplementary analysis of the test-phase likeability
ratings (Table 3) showed a significant main effect of
behavioral history [F(2,94)=12.79, p<.01, η2=.21]. Cheater
faces were less likeable than other faces [F(1,95)=24.83,
pb.01, η2=.21], whereas likeability did not differ between
faces associated with irrelevant and trustworthy behavior
[F(1,95)=1.56, p=.21, η2=.02]. Faces associated with
exceptional and ordinary behavior were equally likable
[F(1,95)=0.14, p=.71, η2b.01]. There was no interaction
between both variables [F(2,94)=0.06, p=.94, η2b.01].

We analyzed the difference in rated attractiveness of the
focal cartoon task and the interrupting 10-minute survey in
a 2 # 2 ANCOVA. We used the initial difference score
from earlier ratings of the tasks as a covariate. We found a
signiﬁcant effect of the task attractiveness covariate (b p
.527, F(1, 164) = 14.306, = = .000) and a main effect of
progress on a speciﬁc cartoon (F(1, 164) = 5.018, = =
.026). We found no main effect of whether the interruption
came during the ﬁrst or second of the two cartoons in the
cartoon task nor a two-way interaction (all F ! 1). Mean
differences (attractiveness of interruption – attractiveness
of continuing cartoon task) for the four interruption points
(M25% ﬁrst cartoon p .725, M75% ﬁrst cartoon p .700, M25% second
cartoon p .682, M75% second cartoon p .444) revealed no linear
(F ! 1, p p .335) nor quadratic trend (F ! 1, p p .755)
but a cubic trend of overall progress on the task of com-
pleting two cartoons (F(1, 164) = 5.02, = = .045). This
nonmonotonic pattern implies that the psychologically rel-
evant aspect of the interruption was its nearness to com-
